overview: This bill, called the READ Act, updates a federal grant program that helps states improve reading and writing instruction from early childhood through high school. It ties the program to the "science of reading," a body of research emphasizing explicit teaching of skills like phonics (sounding out words), vocabulary and comprehension, and it bars funded instruction from relying on "three-cueing," a method that teaches children to guess words from pictures or context. States receiving grants would screen all students for reading difficulties, including dyslexia, at least once before third grade, offer help such as small-group tutoring and summer programs, notify parents when a child is behind, review teacher training programs, and publish yearly progress reports; at least 75 percent of the money would go to local school districts and other groups. States ranking in the bottom fifth nationally on fourth-grade reading scores on the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP, often called the Nation's Report Card) would be guaranteed grants if they apply. The bill also funds reading research through the Education Department's research arm and requires quick state-by-state NAEP reports, while barring the Education Secretary from dictating curriculum. As of August 6, 2026, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say the bill steers federal reading money toward teaching methods backed by research, catches struggling readers early, and keeps parents informed, with extra help for the states that need it most.
against: Critics say federal grant rules that favor one teaching approach and ban others push the national government into classroom decisions usually left to states, teachers and local schools.
